title: The Westminster Confession Chapter 9: Of Free Will
speaker: Unknown Speaker
summary: This lesson introduces a 13-part series on the Christian life from regeneration to glorification, focusing on Westminster Confession Chapter 9 concerning the freedom of the human will. The speaker explains that the will is free from external coercion but bound to one's nature or heart, and examines how the will functions in four states: before the fall (able to sin or not sin), after the fall (unable not to sin), after regeneration (able not to sin), and in glory (unable to sin).

outline.title: Introduction to Free Will and the Nature of the Will
subpoints: The will determines what a person will do based on understanding and natural inclinations
The will is bound only to one's nature or heart, not external forces
Liberty and ability are distinct concepts—one can be free to choose without having the ability to do it
The will operates perfectly; the issue is the corrupt nature that feeds it

outline.title: The Will Before the Fall: Posse Peccare, Posse Non Peccare
subpoints: Adam had freedom and power to will and do good pleasing to God
His will was mutable—he had the ability both to sin and not to sin
He was able to choose either obedience or disobedience

outline.title: The Will After the Fall: Non Posse Non Peccare
subpoints: The natural man has wholly lost ability to will any spiritual good accompanying salvation
The natural man cannot and will not choose God—it is inconsistent with his sinful nature
Spiritual deadness makes it impossible for man to convert himself
The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit and cannot know them

outline.title: The Will of the Regenerate Person: Posse Non Peccare
subpoints: God converts the sinner and translates him into the state of grace
The regenerate person is freed from natural bondage under sin and enabled by grace to will spiritual good
The regenerate can choose to obey or disobey God due to remaining corruption
Spiritual struggle with sin is evidence of spiritual life, not spiritual death

outline.title: The Will in Glory: Non Posse Peccare
subpoints: The will is made perfectly and immutably free to do good alone in the state of glory
This state is better than Adam's before the fall—we will be unable to sin
In eternity, we will not need to work at not sinning
We will be like Christ and see Him as He is

outline.title: Practical Applications of Free Will Doctrine
subpoints: This doctrine should humble us before God—salvation is entirely of grace
We should depend completely upon God's grace rather than trying harder on our own
We should pray expectantly for the salvation of unbelievers since only God changes hearts
We should evangelize faithfully, knowing salvation is God's work, not ours
We should be encouraged in our struggles, recognizing them as evidence of the Spirit's presence

outline.title: The Heart as the True Problem and God's Grace as the True Solution
subpoints: Our greatest problem is not lack of information but a corrupt heart
Our greatest hope is not stronger determination but the sovereign grace of God
Education is not the solution to all evils; the gospel is
God transforms our hearts by His Spirit and will perfect our wills in glory

transcript:
## Introduction and Series Overview

I hope everybody has all their fingers left after yesterday. It's good to see everyone. We are starting a new 13-part series today, going from regeneration all the way to glorification. There will be several of us teaching this series. We will use the confession story in Chapter 9 to guide us through this series. I hope you'll be able to be here for all of it.

You can see that the work continues here on the building. They left Thursday and stopped working, so we had to have them come back yesterday to reposition their equipment and get access to the parking lot. The waterline installation is what they're working on now. The city inspector had to approve the work before they could continue.

## Opening the Westminster Confession Chapter 9

I would love for you to grab a hymnal and turn to the back using the page numbers to page 854. That is where you will find Chapter 9 of the Westminster Confession of Faith, which is titled "Of Free Will." I'm going to read the whole chapter and then we're going to consider it as we go through this series. Our goal is to get through the five paragraphs of this chapter today.

### Full Reading of Chapter 9

> "God has endued the will of man with that natural liberty, that is neither forced nor by any absolute necessity of nature determined to do good or evil. Man, in his state of innocence, had freedom and power to will and to do that which was good and well pleasing to God, but yet mutably so that he might fall from it. Man, by his fall into a state of sin, has wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation. So as a natural man being altogether averse from that good and dead in sin is not able by his own strength to convert himself or to prepare himself thereunto. When God converts a sinner and translates him into the state of grace, he frees him from his natural bondage under sin and by his grace alone enables him freely to will and to do that which is spiritually good. Yet so as that by reason of his remaining corruption, he does not perfectly nor only will that which is good, but does also will that which is evil. The will of man is made perfect and immutably free to good alone in the state of glory only." (Westminster Confession of Faith, Chapter 9)

## Understanding the Nature and Function of the Will

### What is the Will?

The will is that part of the human mind which determines what a person will do. The will makes a decision based on two things: the understanding of the situation, or what you know about what's going on, and the will's reading of the person's natural inclination and priorities—the person's nature.

Our will is truly free and is not absolutely submitted to anything outside of ourselves. The only thing our will is bound to is our nature—we will not choose or act contrary to who we are.

### Nature Equals Heart

Another word for nature, and the one used most in the Bible, is heart. The heart is the way that the Bible speaks about our nature, of who we truly are, the core of our being.

We see this in the Scriptures. The Lord Jesus says in Luke:

> "A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good. Out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. And the evil man out of the evil treasure of the heart brings forth evil." (Luke 6:45)

In Proverbs, the Holy Spirit says:

> "Keep your heart with all diligence for out of it springs all the issues of life." (Proverbs 4:23)

Everything we choose comes from our heart, not from anywhere else. We are not absolutely bound to anything outside of ourselves—only to our own heart as far as our will goes.

### The Meaning of Free Will

When we say the will is free, we mean that the will is free to express a person's nature. The will is free to do what you want to do in your heart, to express who you are. We do not mean that the will is free to choose what is right, because the will is not forced to act contrary to the person's nature.

Nature is stronger than knowledge. How many times do we make decisions that are contrary to what we know about Christ, even as redeemed people? That is what we call sin—decisions contrary to who Christ is and what God wants for us.

### Liberty vs. Ability

One of the most helpful distinctions comes from A. A. Hodge in his book *Outlines of Theology*. He defines liberty and ability:

**Liberty** consists in the power of the agent to will as he pleases from the fact that the volition is determined only by the character of the agent willing. We have complete freedom and liberty.

But liberty is not the same as ability. For example, if someone chooses to fly by stepping on the roof and letting go, they are free to make that decision, but they do not have the ability to do what they chose to do.

**Ability** consists in the power of the agent to change his own subjective state, to make himself prefer what he does not prefer, and to act in a given case in opposition to the coexistent desires and preferences of the agent's own heart.

Hodge concludes: "Thus man is truly free since the fall as before it, because he wills as his evil heart pleases. But he has lost all ability to obey the law of God because his evil heart is not subject to that law. Neither can he change it."

Freedom and ability are two different things, and we need to keep that in mind. You can be free to choose something while not being able to do the thing that you choose to do. We can make choices between coconut ice cream and chocolate ice cream, between Coke Zero and Diet Coke. But we are talking about moral choices when discussing the will. The distinction is between choices that are not themselves moral and choices that are moral.

## The Four States of the Will

### Paragraph 1: The Will Is Free from External Coercion

In the first paragraph, the Westminster Confession teaches us that man's will is free from any exterior pressure. The keyword is "absolute." There is no absolute necessity of nature. Nothing from the outside can make us do something.

> "God has endured the will of man with that natural liberty that is neither forced nor by any absolute necessity of nature determined to do good or evil." (Westminster Confession of Faith, Chapter 9, Paragraph 1)

The will itself, by creative design, is not the problem. The will is like a machine—it's working perfectly. Whatever you put in, whatever the raw material is, will dictate what the output is. It is not the will that needs to be changed in us. It is something else that needs to be changed in us—what pushes the will, what feeds the will—and that is our nature.

The Lord Jesus speaks of this in Matthew:

> "Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or else make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for a tree is known by its fruit. Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things, and an evil man out of the evil treasure brings forth evil things." (Matthew 12:33-35)

Our sin does not come from Satan making us do it, or our spouse, or our kids. James explains:

> "Each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own desires." (James 1:14)

It is not outside influences that absolutely make us sin—it is our nature pushing the will that the Lord has given us.

### Paragraph 2: The Will Before the Fall

Paragraph two talks about the will of man before the fall:

> "Man, in his state of innocence, had freedom and power to will and to do that which was good and well pleasing to God, but yet mutably so that he might fall from it." (Westminster Confession of Faith, Chapter 9, Paragraph 2)

Before the fall, man could do good and he could do evil. He was able to do either of those things. He was able to please God. God made men upright, but he also gave them a changeable will and a changeable nature. We know that was a changeable state simply because it changed—we have the account in Genesis chapter 3.

### Paragraph 3: The Will After the Fall

Paragraph three talks about the will after the fall, the unregenerate will:

> "Man, by his fall into a state of sin, has wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation. So as a natural man being altogether averse from that good and dead in sin is not able by his own strength to convert himself or to prepare himself thereunto." (Westminster Confession of Faith, Chapter 9, Paragraph 3)

The natural man after the fall cannot will salvation. Romans 5:6 says:

> "For when we were still without strength, Christ died for the ungodly." (Romans 5:6)

But it is not just that he cannot. The natural man will not choose God because it is inconsistent with his nature. Romans 3:10-12 says:

> "As it is written: 'There is none righteous, no, not one; there is none who understands; there is none who seeks God.'" (Romans 3:10-12)

No natural man on his own is seeking God. Man is dead as far as choosing to believe in God through Jesus Christ. The apostle says in Ephesians 2:1:

> "And you He made alive, who were dead in trespasses and sins." (Ephesians 2:1)

This deadness makes it impossible for man to convert himself. Listen to what Paul says in 1 Corinthians 2:14:

> "But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned." (1 Corinthians 2:14)

The natural man apart from the work of the Spirit will not come to God. It is not just that he cannot—he will not. He does not want to, and he does not have the ability to do so.

### Paragraph 4: The Will of the Regenerate Person

In section four, we have the will of the converted person, the regenerate person. Paragraph four says:

> "When God converts a sinner and translates him into the state of grace, he frees him from his natural bondage under sin, and by his grace alone enables him freely to will and to do that which is spiritually good. Yet so that by reason of his remaining corruption, he does not perfectly, nor only will that which is good, but does also will that which is evil." (Westminster Confession of Faith, Chapter 9, Paragraph 4)

The saved person can choose to do good or choose to do evil. He can choose to obey God or choose to disobey God. There remains remaining corruption until glory.

Our experience of struggle with sin is not uncommon—it is the common experience of believers. The presence of spiritual conflict is often evidence of spiritual life. The struggle is evidence of the presence of the Spirit. A lack of struggle with sin is concerning.

When we speak of struggle, we mean fighting, going against. Struggling does not simply mean wanting to do something; it means resisting it. If someone says they are struggling with pornography but then admits they viewed it last night, they are not struggling—they are indulging. The struggle is the fight, and the fight is evidence of the presence of the Spirit.

The unbeliever loves sin without conflict, but the believer increasingly hates sin even while battling it. We are encouraged by this doctrine. Even in our state of being regenerated by God, the struggle is there, but it is the common experience of all believers and how we become more like Jesus Christ.

### Paragraph 5: The Will in Glory

Finally, we come to the fifth section, paragraph five, which speaks of man's will in glory when he is perfected:

> "The will of man is made perfectly and immutably free to do good alone in the state of glory only." (Westminster Confession of Faith, Chapter 9, Paragraph 5)

Do you realize that this is a better state than Adam before the fall? Because Adam before the fall could sin and could not sin. But in eternity, we will not be able to sin. The apostle John says:

> "Behold, now we are children of God; and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be. But we know that when He is revealed, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is." (1 John 3:2)

We are going to be like Christ and not able to sin anymore. That is the glory of heaven, which is greater than the glory of the garden.

### The Four States in Latin Terminology

Historically, theologians have categorized these four states using Latin terms:

1. **Before the fall**: *Posse peccare, posse non peccare*—able to sin, able not to sin. That is what humanity was before the fall.

2. **Following the fall**: *Non posse non peccare*—not able not to sin. A natural man is not able not to sin. Even the everyday activities of the wicked are an abomination before God because they are tainted with their own sin.

3. **Once a person is regenerate**: *Posse non peccare*—able not to sin. The regenerate person has the ability to resist sin through God's grace.

4. **In eternity**: *Non posse peccare*—not able to sin anymore. What a glorious state that will be! It will not take work not to sin in that place. In this life it takes a lot of work to not sin and to live in righteousness by God's grace, but in glory, we will be unable to sin.

## Practical Applications

### Application 1: Humility Before God

This doctrine should humble us before God. If our wills are bound to our nature, then no one can boast that he chose Christ because he was wiser or more spiritual or more virtuous than someone else. All of us were at some point in rebellion against God. We cannot boast that Christ chose us because we are smarter or more intelligent, because we are all dead in our trespasses and our sins.

Salvation is entirely of grace. Every believer should be marked by humility rather than pride. We should regularly thank God for giving us a new heart that now enables our will to choose Him.

### Application 2: Complete Dependence on God's Grace

We should depend completely upon God's grace. Many people believe that they simply need to try harder to become a Christian or to please God or to be a better person. But this lesson reminds us that we do not merely need better habits. We need a new heart. It is not rearranging the furniture on the outside—that would be equivalent to rearranging the deck furniture on the Titanic as it is going down. It is pointless. Only the Holy Spirit can give spiritual life. This should make us rely upon God's grace every day instead of our own strength.

### Application 3: Expectant Prayer for the Unbelievers

This doctrine should lead us to pray expectantly for the salvation of unbelievers. If conversion depended on human will alone, we would have very little reason to pray. But because God changes hearts, we can pray confidently for unbelieving family members, for our children, for neighbors, for coworkers. We never give up on someone because no heart is too hard for God.

This doctrine leads us into evangelistic prayer rather than discouraging it. Christians are often inconsistent in their beliefs. You can be in a big argument with somebody who does not believe that God is sovereign in salvation, who thinks that people can choose God on their own. Yet when you get on your knees with them to pray for people, guess what they pray for? They pray that God would save those people. In what we pray and what we sing, a doctrine other than the sovereignty of God just does not lend itself to praying and singing.

### Application 4: Faithful Evangelism

This doctrine also leads us to evangelize faithfully. Some object that God's sovereignty discourages evangelism, but the opposite is true. Since only God can change hearts, we proclaim Christ, we lovingly persuade sinners, and then we leave the result to God. This frees you to evangelism because the salvation of people is not on your shoulders. You are not in charge of saving that person. You can just present the gospel, give them the gospel, be persuasive and winsome, and God is the one that does it.

Our confidence rests not in persuasive techniques but in the power of the Holy Spirit. We are responsible for proclaiming the gospel, but we are not responsible for producing conversions. This was a big misunderstanding during the second Great Awakening. Charles Finney, a Presbyterian minister, thought that he could psychologically create an environment that would produce true conversions. He believed it was completely up to the minister and the church to create what happens so that true conversions would occur, and that we did not need the Holy Spirit to do that. That is not what the Bible teaches. Conversions are not up to us. Conversions are up to the Spirit. We just proclaim the word.

### Application 5: Encouragement in Our Struggles

This lesson encourages us in our struggles. Those who are believers often become discouraged because they still battle sin. But paragraph four reminds us that we have a new nature and yet remaining corruption continues until glory. Our experience of struggle is not uncommon—it is the common experience of believers. The presence of spiritual conflict is often evidence of spiritual life. The struggle is evidence of the presence of the Spirit.

The unbeliever loves sin without conflict, but the believer increasingly hates sin even while battling it. We are encouraged by this doctrine that even in our state of being regenerated by God, the struggle is there, and it is how we become more like Jesus Christ.

## The Heart as the True Issue

The doctrine of free will is not merely an abstract theological discussion. It teaches us that our greatest problem is not a lack of information but a corrupt heart. Our greatest hope is not stronger determination but the sovereign grace of God.

Our society thinks, and this is a worldwide phenomenon, that education is a solution to all evils. If you can just educate people more, surely all problems will be solved. But the solution for all evils is the gospel of Jesus Christ because it is the heart that needs to be changed. The God who raised us from spiritual death continues to transform our hearts by His Spirit. One day He will perfect our wills in glory so that we will delight in Him forever.

Are you looking forward to that? Until that day, let us humbly depend upon His grace, faithfully proclaim His gospel, diligently fight sin, and joyfully wait the day when we shall be like Christ. That is going to be a glorious day.
